dataset.name: SPRUCE Aboveground Vegetation Coverage in Root Ingrowth Core Plots, Marcell Experimental Forest, Minnesota, August 2022
description: This dataset contains vegetation survey measurements from root ingrowth core plots (Määttä et al. 2025) inside SPRUCE Experiment plots at the Marcell Experimental Forest in northern Minnesota. Vegetation surveys were conducted in 0.25 meter2 plots containing root ingrowth cores on August 8th and 9th, 2022 (2022-08-08 to 2022-08-09). The warming and elevated carbon dioxide (CO2) treatments in the dataset include the full treatment gradient: +0 degrees Celsius (C) (+0 and +500 parts per million (ppm) elevated CO2), +2.25 degrees C (+0 and +500 ppm), +4.5 degrees C (+0 and +500 ppm elevated CO2), +6.75 degrees C (+0 and +500 ppm) and +9 degrees C (+0 and +500 ppm elevated CO2) for both hummocks and hollows. This dataset includes measurements of the height and absolute coverage (%) for each vascular plant and moss species, as well as organic litter and dead overstory vascular plants, and the distance from the grid center to the nearest tree and the species of the nearest tree. These data were used as species-specific aboveground plant metadata for assessing the warming and elevated CO2 response of fine roots across different peatland microtopographical features (hummocks and hollows) and plant functional types (shrub, spruce and larch).

This dataset contains one data file in comma separate (.csv) format. Additional metadata are provided: one data dictionary and a file-level metadata file in comma separate (.csv) format and a user guide in PDF (*.pdf) format.

measurementTechnique:
Study Site
Observations occurred at The Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s SPRUCE (Spruce and Peatland Responses Under Changing Environments) project (Hanson et al., 2017) at S1 bog at the U.S. Forest Service’s Marcell Experimental Forest, in Minnesota, USA (47°30.476’ N; 93°27.162’ W). SPRUCE is an ecosystem-scale study that warms the vegetation and peatland soil profile to a depth of 2 m within 12.8-m diameter open-top enclosures. The peat was heated first at – 2 m for a period of 1 year starting in summer 2014 (deep peat heating phase), then heating of the overlying air began in August 2015 starting the whole ecosystem warming phase of the experiment.

Methods
In June 2022, root ingrowth core sets A and B were installed in each of the 12 experimental SPRUCE plots (with and without enclosures, Määttä et al. 2025). Vegetation coverages per each set (A or B) were done so that both root ingrowth cores (one in hummock and one in hollow) were inside the grid.
The vegetation survey was conducted with the visual cover estimation method. A survey grid (49.5 x 50 cm) was used for estimating the absolute coverage of each found vascular plant species and moss order or genus within the grid area. In addition, the percentage coverage of organic litter and dead aboveground vegetation was estimated.
The grid was set around the root ingrowth cores so that the cores would be approximately at the center of the grid, in order to cover the species composition around them. Therefore, one grid was used to cover both a hummock and a hollow simultaneously. In cases where both root ingrowth cores did not fit into the grid, the grid was set in between them. The position of the grid in relation to its surroundings was kept constant by keeping the bottom edge parallel to the boardwalk. The area of the cores (max 2 x root ingrowth cores and max 2 x fungal cores; number of cores varies between A and B sets and plots) was not counted to the 100% coverage area, therefore the area considered for the coverage was A[grid] - A[cores] (1 x A[core] = 41.85 cm2).
In addition to species, moss, organic litter and dead overstory vascular plant coverage, the height of each found vascular plant species (not trees) was estimated by dividing the grid into four even squares using two strings, setting a dowel at the center of each of the four squares, and measuring the height of the tallest plant touching the dowel. This was repeated for all of the four squares and the center point of the large grid, resulting in 5 height measurements per grid. The 5 measurements were then used to calculate the average height per species per set (A or B) per plot. The distance of the grid center to the nearest tagged tree was measured and the species and ID of the tree was recorded. Tree IDs can be found in Hanson et al. (2018).
